title: UseMoney — workers performance
description: managed-by:apply-dashboards — edit the file, not the UI

definition._why: States the two things a reader cannot infer from the graphs: where these series come from (so a gap is a vendor question, not a missing emitter) and why no selector applies to them.
definition.content: Every series here is supplied by the GCP integration (MONEY-1379) and preflighted by apply-perf-monitors.sh before any monitor exists over it. No env tag on gcp.* — scoped by name. LLM Observability widgets land in the phase-2 PR once ml_obs.* has been observed (MONEY-1380).

definition.title: Pub/Sub — oldest unacked message age, top 10 (s)
definition._why: Answers 'is any queue about to redeliver'. At 600s Pub/Sub gives up waiting and hands the SAME message to a second container, so the work doubles rather than fails — the only symptom is this line crossing the red marker. Top 10 because 190 subscriptions exist and the *-pull-local ones are never drained, so an unscoped chart is permanently red and therefore permanently ignored.

definition.title: Pub/Sub — the 12 analysis/LLM subscriptions, oldest unacked (s)
definition._why: Answers the same question for the handlers that call a MODEL, which is where an overrun is expected rather than surprising. Named explicitly instead of pattern-matched so a new analysis subscription is an edit here, not a silent omission from the one chart that would have shown it.

definition.title: Pub/Sub — undelivered messages by subscription
definition._why: Answers 'how much work is waiting', which age alone cannot tell you: one stuck message and ten thousand queued messages both show as an old oldest-unacked, and only one of them means the workers are under-provisioned.

definition.title: Dead-lettered (24h)
definition._why: Answers 'did anything get thrown away'. A dead-letter is the end of the line — five delivery attempts exhausted — so any non-zero value is work that will never be done unless somebody replays it, which is why the format goes red at >0 rather than at a threshold.

definition.title: Pub/Sub — push responses by class (stacked)
definition._why: Answers 'is the delivery itself healthy', one layer below the handler's own counters. Pub/Sub ACKs only on a 2xx, so a wall of remote_server_5xx here is a redelivery loop building up before any job-level metric moves.

definition.title: Pub/Sub — 5xx + unreachable by subscription (1h)
definition._why: Answers 'which subscription is failing', which the stacked chart above deliberately hides by grouping on response class. `unreachable` sits beside 5xx because a service that cannot be reached at all and one that answers 500 are the same outcome for the message.

definition.title: Cloud Run — instances vs cap
definition._why: Answers 'are we out of room'. A service pinned at its maxScale is not scaling any more — the queue behind it grows instead, so this is the chart that explains an unacked age that will not come down. The two markers are the two different caps; one line at 20 would be wrong for us-fundamentals.

definition.title: Cloud Run workers — handler time p95 / p99 / avg (ms)
definition._why: Answers 'how close is a handler to the ack deadline' from the SERVICE side, before the queue shows it. UNITS: this series is MILLISECONDS, so the deadline marker is 600000 and not 600 — the same number as the Pub/Sub widget above, three orders of magnitude apart, and a marker copied between them looks entirely plausible while being wrong.

definition.title: Cloud Run workers — pending requests
definition._why: Answers 'is the service holding requests it has not started yet'. Pending is the half-second of truth between Pub/Sub having delivered and a container having begun: a standing queue here means the instance cap is binding even when instance_count looks calm between samples.

definition.title: Cloud Run workers — CPU / memory utilisation p95
definition._why: Answers 'which resource would a bigger instance buy back'. The doc-conversion pass died twice on 'The configured memory limit was reached' while CPU sat idle — two very different remedies, and a single 'saturation' number cannot tell them apart.

definition.title: Cloud Run workers — requests by response class
definition._why: Answers 'what is the service actually returning'. This is the same population as the Pub/Sub push chart seen from the other end, and the two disagreeing is itself the finding: a 2xx here with a 5xx there is a delivery problem, not a handler one.

definition.title: Cloud Run workers — cold-start latency p95 (ms)
definition._why: Answers 'how much of a handler's budget is spent before its own code runs'. A cold start is charged to the SAME 600s ack deadline as the work, so a startup regression eats headroom from every job at once without appearing in any job's own timing. Milliseconds, like every gcp.run latency series.

definition.title: Cloud Run workers — max request concurrency p95
definition._why: Answers 'how many messages one container is chewing at once', which is the multiplier on every memory and CPU number above. It is also the lever: lowering concurrency buys per-request headroom without raising the instance cap.

definition.title: Gemini — input-token quota utilisation by model
definition._why: Answers 'how close are we to being refused'. The requests-per-minute quota limit is INT64_MAX — unlimited — so TOKENS are the only real ceiling Google enforces, which is why this is the widget with thresholds and the one below it has none. Plotted as usage/limit so a quota increase moves the ceiling rather than invalidating the markers.

definition.title: Gemini — requests/min by model (no ceiling)
definition._why: Answers 'which model is being called, and how much', as a shape to read the token chart against — deliberately with NO markers, because this quota's limit is INT64_MAX and a threshold drawn over an unlimited ceiling is a number somebody will later mistake for a real one.

definition.title: Cloud Scheduler — failed attempts by job (executions log)
definition._why: Answers 'did a job even get triggered'. A scheduler attempt that ends DEADLINE_EXCEEDED never reaches Pub/Sub at all, so every other widget on this board stays perfectly calm while the work silently does not happen — the one failure here that is invisible from inside the workers.
